```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(AKCatchments)
options(AKCatchments.cache = file.path(tempdir(), "ak_vignette_cache"))
```

Projected change in monthly and seasonal temperature and precipitation for
each catchment, model and emissions scenario, from SNAP's (Scenarios
Network for Alaska + Arctic Planning, University of Alaska Fairbanks)
daily CMIP6 downscaling: 4 km, 1965-2100, bias-adjusted by quantile delta
mapping against WRF-downscaled ERA5; up to 13 models and four SSP
scenarios (`ak_climate_projection_models()`). `source = "snap_cmip6_4km"` is the only
source so far.

Input, as for every layer: catchments (sf polygons with `site_code`, one
row per catchment, any CRS; a single `ak_delineate()` result, a list of
them, `ak_catchments()` output or your own polygons). Chunks that download
data are not run when this vignette is built; chunks that only compute
are. The other layers are listed in `vignette("delineation")`, section 7.

## 1. Getting the data

Automatic: SNAP's rasdaman server is queried directly, one request per
variable, model, run and block of nearby catchments, and the monthly mean
of each 4 km cell is cached in `snap_cmip6/` (one file per variable,
model and run), so other catchments in the same cells and a shared cache
reuse it. Requests are 1-5 MB; a default run for a few hundred catchments
is hundreds of requests and can take hours. A progress bar counts the
coverages (variable x model x run); with mirai daemons running they are
fetched in parallel (`?ak_parallel`; 4-6 daemons is plenty for one
server). Failed coverages are reported in `attr(, "failed")`, not fatal.

```{r models}
m <- ak_climate_projection_models()
head(m)
table(m$scenario[m$var == "tasmax" & m$model != "7ModelAvg"])
```

## 2. Using it

```{r use, eval = FALSE}
d <- ak_delineate(lat = 63.7255, lon = -148.9670, site_code = "SITE-001")
dl <- ak_climate_projection(d, scenarios = c("ssp245", "ssp585"),
                            periods = list(`2041-2070` = 2041:2070, `2071-2100` = 2071:2100))
ens <- projection_ensemble(dl)                        # long: site x variable x scenario x period x season

seasons <- c(ak_seasons(), nov_mar = list(c(11, 12, 1, 2, 3)))   # e.g. your winter precipitation window
dl <- ak_climate_projection(d, seasons = seasons, keep_series = TRUE)

x <- ak_catchments(pts)
dl <- ak_climate_projection(x, seasons = ak_seasons(months = FALSE)[c("annual", "jja", "djf")],
                            periods = list(`2041-2070` = 2041:2070))   # per-model table (for propagating model spread)
x <- catchment_join(x, projection_ensemble(dl, wide = TRUE))          # ensemble columns: cmip6_dtmean_jja_ssp245_2041_2070, ...
```

Applying the change to an observed baseline:

```{r apply, eval = FALSE}
x <- ak_climate_normals(x, vars = "tmean", periods = "07")         # prism_tmean_07
fut <- dl |>
  dplyr::filter(var == "tmean", season == "m07", scenario == "ssp245") |>
  dplyr::left_join(sf::st_drop_geometry(x)[c("site_code", "prism_tmean_07")], by = "site_code") |>
  dplyr::mutate(jul_tmean_future = prism_tmean_07 + delta)   # one value per model: keep them all
```

## 3. What you get

`ak_climate_projection()`, a table with one row per site, variable (`tasmax`, `tasmin`, `tmean`,
`pr`), scenario, model, period and season: `baseline_mean`,
`future_mean`, `delta` (°C, or mm for the season), `delta_se`, `ratio` and
`log_ratio_se` (precipitation), `n_base`, `n_fut`, `n_eff_base`,
`n_eff_fut`, `delta_local_sd`, `n_cells`, `coverage_pct`, `subgrid`.

`projection_ensemble()`: `n_models`, `delta`, `delta_se` (between-model SD),
`delta_lo95`, `delta_hi95`, `delta_min`, `delta_max`, `pct`, `pct_se`,
`pct_lo95`, `pct_hi95` (precipitation), `internal_se`, `sign_agree`,
`delta_local_sd`, `n_cells`, `coverage_pct`, `flag`.

`projection_ensemble(dl, wide = TRUE)`, one row per site for
`catchment_join()`: `cmip6_dtmean_<season>_<scenario>_<period>` and
`cmip6_pr_pct_...` with `_se`, `_lo95`, `_hi95`, `_nmodels`, `_flag`, for
every season, scenario and period in `dl` (so choose them in
`ak_climate_projection()`: each combination is five columns).

## 4. Uncertainty: how it is computed

**What is delivered: change, not climate.** SNAP bias-adjusted each model
by quantile delta mapping against WRF-downscaled ERA5, not Daymet, so
absolute projected values differ from the Daymet normals and anomalies
used elsewhere. `ak_climate_projection()` therefore returns each model's change
relative to its own baseline (`delta` in °C or mm; `ratio` for
precipitation), to be added to (or multiplied into) your observed
baseline. Differences between the reference and Daymet cancel; so do each
model's own biases, to first order.

**Sources of uncertainty, and where each goes.**

| source | handled by | column |
|---|---|---|
| scenario (emissions) | kept separate, never averaged | `scenario` |
| model structure | spread across models | `delta_se` (ensemble SD), `delta_lo95`/`hi95`, `delta_min`/`max` |
| internal variability (one run per model) | SE of the difference of two 30-year means | per model `delta_se`, `log_ratio_se`; ensemble `internal_se` |
| spatial: catchment smaller than a 4 km cell | flagged; local spread of the change measured | `subgrid`, `delta_local_sd`, `local_gradient` |
| downscaling and bias adjustment | not quantified | — |

*Internal variability.* With interannual SD s and n years in each period,
SE(Δ) = √(s²_f / n_eff,f + s²_b / n_eff,b), where
n_eff = n (1 − r₁)/(1 + r₁) and r₁ is the lag-1 autocorrelation of the
linearly detrended season-year series (0 if negative). Precipitation is
handled on the log scale: SE(log R) = √(CV²_f / n_eff,f + CV²_b / n_eff,b).
A unit test checks this SE against the spread of simulated differences.

*Model spread.* Models are an ensemble of opportunity: not independent
(several share components), not a random sample. The ensemble SD is a
guide to structural uncertainty, not a probability. The 95% limits are a
prediction interval for one more model treated as exchangeable,
mean ± t₀.₉₇₅,ₙ₋₁ · SD · √(1 + 1/n), which is wider than the range when
there are few models; `few_models` flags fewer than 5. The model's sampling
noise is already part of the spread; `noise_dominated` flags where it is
at least half of it (common for seasonal precipitation).

*Sub-grid catchments.* Most CAKN catchments are smaller than a 4 km cell.
Absolute climate varies strongly within a cell (elevation), but the
*change* varies little, which is why deltas are the product. The SD of
the per-cell change over the catchment's cells and their eight neighbours
(`delta_local_sd`) measures how much the change varies at that scale;
`local_gradient` flags where it exceeds half the ensemble SD.

**Downstream.** For posterior predictions under future climate, push each
model's delta (the per-model table from `ak_climate_projection()`) through the
fitted model, so the model spread propagates; using the ensemble mean
alone hides it. Keep scenarios separate.

**Alternatives.** Kim et al. (2025) provide 10 km daily downscaling of 23
CMIP6 models for Alaska with several bias-correction methods (an ensemble
over methods as well as models); SNAP's 12 km CMIP6 indicators and its
dynamically downscaled WRF runs are other options. The between-product
spread would add the downscaling uncertainty not included here.

## 5. Checking and validating it

- **Baseline against observations.** `baseline_mean` is the downscaled
  models' own 1991-2020 climate, built on ERA5-WRF. It won't equal Daymet
  or PRISM, but across sites it should correlate closely with them; a
  site far off the line is a cell or orientation problem, not climate:

```{r check, eval = FALSE}
b <- dl |> dplyr::filter(var == "tmean", season == "m07") |>
  dplyr::summarise(snap_jul = mean(baseline_mean), .by = site_code)
dplyr::inner_join(b, sf::st_drop_geometry(ak_climate_normals(x, vars = "tmean", periods = "07")), by = "site_code") |>
  with(plot(prism_tmean_07, snap_jul))
```

- **Historical trend.** With `keep_series = TRUE`, the models' trend over
  1991-2020 can be compared with Daymet's observed trend; models are not
  expected to match year to year, only in rate.
- **Requests.** Check `attr(dl, "failed")` and the live tests G06-G07,
  which confirm the server's layout and units.

## 6. Pitfalls

- Use deltas, not absolute projected values.
- Don't average scenarios; don't use only the ensemble mean downstream.
- Model availability differs by scenario and variable (CESM2 has
  precipitation only): `n_models` differs between columns.
- Most catchments are smaller than a 4 km cell (`subgrid`).

## References

- Cannon, A. J., Sobie, S. R. and Murdock, T. Q. (2015). Bias correction of GCM precipitation by quantile mapping. Journal of Climate 28, 6938-6959.
- Eyring, V. et al. (2016). Overview of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6). Geoscientific Model Development 9, 1937-1958.
- Kim, T. et al. (2025). Ensemble downscaled climate dataset for Alaska and Hawaii under historical and future conditions. Scientific Data 12, 1089.
- Lavoie, J. et al. (2024). ESPO-G6-R2: bias-adjusted CMIP6 simulations for North America. Scientific Data, doi:10.1038/s41597-023-02855-z.
- SNAP CMIP6 downscaling code: https://github.com/ua-snap/cmip6-downscaling.
